subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Tissue Preparation — Fixation, Processing and Microtomy

subjective.question: Describe the eyepiece and objective lens of a microscope.
subjective.answer: Eyepiece: An eyepiece is that part of an optical system which is directed to the viewer. It is a construction of one or more lenses. Its function is to convert the real, enlarged intermediate image from the objective into an enlarged virtual image. It contains the ocular lens, which the user looks through to see the magnified specimen; the ocular lens has a magnification ranging from 5x to 30x, but 10x or 15x is the most common setting. Objective lens: The objective is that part of the optical system which is directed to the object; its task is to collect the light rays reflected from the observed item and it generates a real optical image. It combines with the eyepiece lens to increase magnification levels. Microscopes generally feature three or four objective lenses with magnification levels ranging from 4x to 100x, carried on an objective revolver (nosepiece).

subjective.question: What are the limitations of light microscopy?
subjective.answer: (1) Very low contrast of most biological samples. (2) The practical limit to magnification with a light microscope is around 1300X; although higher magnifications are possible, it becomes increasingly difficult to maintain image clarity as magnification increases. (3) Low apparent optical resolution due to the material used. (4) Samples that are naturally colourless and transparent cannot be seen well, e.g. many types of mammalian cells; such samples often have to be stained before viewing, whereas samples that have their own colour can be seen without preparation.

subjective.question: Which factors affect the resolution of a microscope? Write the formula for the limit of resolution.
subjective.answer: The resolution of a microscope is a function of two factors: (1) the numerical aperture (NA) of the optical components, and (2) the wavelength of light (λ) used to examine the specimen. Limit of resolution: d = λ / 2NA, where d is the minimum distance between any two closest points on the microscopic object which can be resolved into two separate and distinct points on the enlarged image. The smaller the wavelength of light (λ), the greater is its ability to resolve the points on the object into distinctly visible finer details; thus the smaller the wavelength, the greater the resolving power.

subjective.question: Define magnification and resolution. On what factors does magnification depend?
subjective.answer: Magnification is the degree of enlargement of an object produced by the microscope. It depends on three factors: (1) the optical tube length, (2) the focal length of the objective, and (3) the magnifying power of the eyepiece. Resolution (resolving power) is the ability of a microscope to distinguish the details of a given specimen, i.e. to separate two closely placed points as distinct. It increases with higher numerical aperture and shorter wavelength of light.

subjective.question: What is numerical aperture? How does it affect the resolving power of a microscope?
subjective.answer: Numerical aperture (NA) is a number that expresses the ability of a lens to resolve fine details in an object being observed. Light diffracted by the specimen is presented as an inverted cone of half-angle α, and NA depends on this angle and the refractive index of the medium. Higher values of numerical aperture permit increasingly oblique rays to enter the objective front lens, so a lens with a higher NA gathers more diffracted light and gives better resolution. Most objectives in the magnification range of 60x to 100x (and higher) are designed for use with immersion oil to achieve a high numerical aperture.

subjective.question: What is micrometry? Describe the types of micrometers and the role of calibration.
subjective.answer: Micrometry is the science in which measurements of the dimensions of an object being observed under the microscope are taken. Two types of micrometers are used: (1) the stage micrometer — a slide with a known, accurately ruled scale; and (2) the ocular micrometer — a glass disc with 100 equal divisions or lines on it but with no absolute value, which is placed in the eyepiece. Because the ocular micrometer has no absolute value, it must be calibrated: calibration is the comparison of measurement values delivered by a device under test with those of a calibration standard of known accuracy, so the value of each ocular division is determined against the stage micrometer for each objective.

subjective.question: Describe bright-field microscopy and the path of light through the microscope.
subjective.answer: In bright-field microscopy the sample is illuminated from below and observed from above through the eyepiece. White light is used, and contrast in the sample is caused by absorbance of some of the transmitted light in dense areas of the sample. Staining is often required to increase contrast, which prevents its use on live cells in many situations. Bright-field illumination is useful for samples which have an intrinsic colour, for example chloroplasts in plant cells. The light path consists of: (1) a trans-illumination light source, commonly a halogen lamp in the microscope stand; (2) a condenser lens which focuses light from the light source onto the sample; (3) the objective lens, which collects light from the sample and magnifies the image; and (4) oculars and/or a camera to view the sample image.

subjective.question: What is dark-field microscopy? Give its principle.
subjective.answer: Dark-field microscopy is the type of microscopy in which only the specimen is lit by a light or electron beam and the rest of the specimen field remains dark. A special condenser blocks the central light so that only oblique rays, scattered or diffracted by the specimen, enter the objective. The specimen therefore appears bright against a dark background, which makes it useful for viewing live, unstained and transparent specimens that are almost invisible in bright-field.

subjective.question: Write a note on phase contrast microscopy.
subjective.answer: Phase contrast microscopy was first described in 1934 by Fritz Zernike, who was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1953 for this work. It is particularly important in biology because it reveals many cellular structures and allows living cells to be observed in their natural state without previously being killed, fixed and stained. Light passing through one material into another material of slightly different refractive index or thickness undergoes a change in phase; these phase changes are invisible to the eye. With the help of a phase ring (annular diaphragm and phase plate), the phase contrast microscope converts invisible small phase changes caused by the cell components into visible intensity (amplitude) changes, seen as different shades of grey. There are two main types: positive and negative phase contrast.

subjective.question: What is electron microscopy? Describe its types and the advantages of SEM.
subjective.answer: Electron microscopy (EM) is a technique for obtaining high-resolution images of biological and non-biological specimens. The high resolution of EM images results from the use of electrons, whose wavelength is much shorter than that of light; EM images provide key information on the structural basis of cell function and of cell disease. There are two types: Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) and Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM). Advantages of SEM: (1) it has a large depth of field, which allows more of a specimen to be in focus at one time; (2) it has much higher resolution, so closely spaced specimens can be magnified at much higher levels; (3) because the SEM uses electromagnets rather than lenses, the researcher has much more control over the degree of magnification; (4) it provides strikingly clear images, making it one of the most useful instruments in research today.

subjective.question: How is a specimen prepared for transmission electron microscopy (TEM)?
subjective.answer: Since electrons are deflected by air molecules and are easily absorbed and scattered by solid matter, only extremely thin slices (20 to 100 nm) of a specimen can be viewed in an average TEM. Such a thin slice cannot be cut unless the specimen has support of some kind; the necessary support is provided by plastic. The steps are: (1) fixation with chemicals like glutaraldehyde or osmium tetroxide to stabilize cell structure; (2) dehydration with organic solvents (e.g. acetone or ethanol) — complete dehydration is essential because most plastics used for embedding are not water soluble; (3) the specimen is soaked in unpolymerized liquid epoxy plastic until it is completely permeated; (4) the plastic is hardened to form a solid block; and (5) thin sections are cut from this block with a glass or diamond knife using a special instrument called an ultramicrotome. Other preparation techniques include negative staining and shadowing, in which a specimen is coated with a thin film of platinum or other heavy metal by evaporation at an angle of about 45° from horizontal.

subjective.question: Write a short note on fluorescence microscopy.
subjective.answer: Fluorescence microscopy is a critical tool for academic and pharmaceutical research, pathology and clinical medicine. Its key feature is that it employs reflected rather than transmitted light. The specimen is first labelled with a fluorescent dye/substance known as a fluorophore, and the microscope is used for tracing the location of a specific protein in the specimen. A fluorescence microscope includes a set of compatible optical filters: an excitation filter, which selects the wavelengths to excite a particular dye within the specimen, an emission filter, and a dichroic beam splitter, which is an optical device that splits a beam of light in two. A xenon arc lamp, a highly specialized type of gas discharge lamp, is commonly used as the light source. TIRFM (Total Internal Reflection Fluorescence Microscopy) is a specialized form of this technique.

subjective.topic: Tissue Preparation — Fixation, Processing and Microtomy
subjective.question: What is fixation? Name the commonly used fixatives and the properties of an ideal fixative.
subjective.answer: Fixation is the process of preserving the tissues in their natural condition. Poorly fixed specimens are more difficult to section than well-fixed ones. Commonly used fixatives are alcohol, formalin and glutaraldehyde; commonly 10% formalin or 2.5% glutaraldehyde is used. Coagulant fixatives include 50–60% ethanol and 80% methanol, while picric acid and trichloroacetic acid are acidic coagulants. Formaldehyde is a powerful reducing agent, and paraformaldehyde depolymerises back to formalin when heated. An ideal fixative should be non-toxic and non-allergenic, should penetrate the tissue adequately (mercurials such as Zenker's fixative penetrate poorly and produce tissue shrinkage) and should preserve the tissue without distortion. Fixation methods are grouped into two: physical methods and chemical methods.

subjective.topic: Tissue Preparation — Fixation, Processing and Microtomy
subjective.question: What is embedding? Why do tissues need an embedding medium?
subjective.answer: Embedding is the process in which the tissues or the specimens are enclosed in a mass of the embedding medium using a mould. Since the tissue blocks are very thin in thickness, they need a supporting medium in which the tissue blocks are embedded; this supporting medium is called the embedding medium. Common embedding media include paraffin wax for routine histology and the OCT (optimum cutting temperature) compound used in cryomicrotomy.

subjective.topic: Tissue Preparation — Fixation, Processing and Microtomy
subjective.question: Differentiate between manual and automated tissue processing.
subjective.answer: Manual processing is the slow, most labour-intensive method, since transfer of specimens or changing of reagents is done by hand; with the advance of automation this method is almost obsolete. Automated processing is of two main types: (1) specimen-transfer or 'dip and dunk' processors — instruments which transfer cassettes from station to station in a rotary or linear configuration; and (2) fluid-transfer or 'enclosed' instruments, which hold the specimens in a process chamber or retort while the reagents are pumped in and out during processing. Microwave-assisted processing might require manual transfer of specimen or reagents, but it accelerates processing by heating the reagents.

subjective.topic: Tissue Preparation — Fixation, Processing and Microtomy
subjective.question: Describe the saw microtome and the laser microtome.
subjective.answer: Saw microtome: It is especially used for hard materials such as teeth or bones. The microtome of this type has a recessed rotating saw which slices through the sample. The minimal cut thickness is approximately 30 μm, and sections can be made for comparatively large samples. Laser microtome: It cuts tissue or other material with the help of photons instead of steel blades. The method is contact-free and enables tissue to be cut in its native state; special preparation techniques are not required. Cutting is by optical breakdown, and the thickness achievable is between 10 and 100 μm.

subjective.topic: Tissue Preparation — Fixation, Processing and Microtomy
subjective.question: What is a cryostat/cryomicrotome? Describe tissue preparation for cryomicrotomy.
subjective.answer: A cryomicrotome is an microtome arranged in a cryostat and used to prepare thin sections of frozen tissue for microscopic examination; the temperature inside the cryostat is about −20° to −30°C. The cryostat is the instrument that has the arrangement both to freeze the tissue and to cut the frozen tissue for microscopic section. For quick freezing it is convenient to process sample sizes not larger than 2 mm so that freezing is homogeneous through all the tissue thickness, including the inner parts, and cryoprotection is always a good practice. In the frozen tissue, the firm ice within the tissue acts as the embedding medium; presently OCT (optimum cutting temperature) compound (Tissue-Tek) is used as the embedding medium to hold the tissue over the chuck.

subjective.topic: Tissue Preparation — Fixation, Processing and Microtomy
subjective.question: Write a note on microtome knives.
subjective.answer: There are four types of microtome knives: steel knives, glass knives, diamond knives and sapphire knives. Steel blades are used to prepare sections of animal or plant tissues for light microscopy histology. Glass knives are used in an ultramicrotome to cut ultrathin slices of samples for electron and light microscope applications. A diamond knife is a very sharp knife in which the edge is made from diamond; it was invented by Humberto Fernández-Morán in 1955 and is used for ultrathin sectioning in electron microscopy. Micron settings for section thickness can range from 1 to 60 microns on most microtomes.

subjective.question: Define separation techniques. Differentiate between homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures.
subjective.answer: Separation techniques are those techniques that can be used to separate two different states of matter, such as liquids and solids. A homogeneous mixture is a mixture that is uniform throughout; for example, air is a homogeneous mixture of different gases including oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide and water vapour. A heterogeneous mixture is a mixture that is not uniform throughout, i.e. the ingredients of the mixture are distributed unequally.

subjective.question: What is centrifugation? Describe its types.
subjective.answer: Centrifugation is a mechanical process which involves the use of centrifugal force for the sedimentation of heterogeneous mixtures with a centrifuge. This process is used to separate two immiscible liquids. A centrifuge is a device for separating particles from a solution according to their size, shape, density and the viscosity of the medium. Types of centrifugation: (1) Differential pelleting (differential centrifugation); (2) Density gradient centrifugation, which is of two types — (i) rate-zonal density-gradient centrifugation and (ii) isopycnic centrifugation; and (3) ultracentrifugation, performed at very high speeds.

subjective.question: Differentiate between hot filtration and cold filtration. What is multilayer filtration?
subjective.answer: Multilayer filtration refers to multiple layers of different material, including sand, gravel or charcoal, where the different layers contain different particle sizes of that material. A mixture of liquid and insoluble solid particles is poured over the layers, and the solid particles are caught throughout, resulting in a filtered liquid. Cold filtration makes use of very low temperatures, often by using an ice bath; some substances, such as fatty acid particles, become suspended in the mixture as they cool down, which then allows them to be filtered out more easily. Hot filtration is often used for crystalline compounds that contain impurities: the crystalline compound is melted down, the impurities are removed while the substance is still in liquid form, and the now-pure substance is finally recrystallized; it is recommended that the apparatus used be heated so that the filtered substance does not crystallize in the funnel and block the flow.

subjective.question: Differentiate between cationic and anionic exchangers.
subjective.answer: Cationic exchangers possess negatively charged groups, and these attract positively charged cations. These exchangers are also called 'acidic ion exchange' materials, because their negative charges result from the ionization of acidic groups. Anionic exchangers have positively charged groups that attract negatively charged anions; these are also called 'basic ion exchange' materials. Ion exchange chromatography is most often performed in the form of column chromatography; however, there are also thin-layer chromatographic methods that work basically on the principle of ion exchange.

subjective.question: What is ethidium bromide? Describe its role in gel electrophoresis.
subjective.answer: Ethidium bromide is a fluorescent intercalating dye, the most convenient and commonly used dye for detecting nucleic acids in gels; it contains a tricyclic planar group that intercalates between the stacked bases of DNA. Intercalation of ethidium bromide causes a decrease in the negative charge of the double-stranded DNA and an increase in both its stiffness and length, and the rate of migration of the linear DNA–dye complex through gels is retarded by about 15%. If ethidium bromide is present in the gel and the electrophoresis buffer, the gel is examined by UV light; UV radiation at 254 nm is absorbed by the DNA and transmitted to the dye. Ethidium bromide can be used to detect both single- and double-stranded nucleic acids (both DNA and RNA).

subjective.question: Describe the factors affecting the rate of migration of DNA through agarose gels.
subjective.answer: (1) Molecular size of DNA: molecules of double-stranded DNA migrate through gel matrices at rates that are inversely proportional to the log10 of the number of base pairs. (2) Conformation of the DNA: superhelical circular (form I), nicked circular (form II) and linear (form III) DNAs migrate at different rates, depending on the concentration and type of agarose, the strength of the applied current, the ionic strength of the buffer and the density of superhelical twists in form I DNA. (3) Ethidium bromide: intercalation decreases the negative charge of dsDNA and increases its stiffness and length, retarding migration by about 15%. (4) Voltage: at low voltages the rate of migration of linear DNA fragments is proportional to the voltage applied, but as the field strength is raised, the mobility of high-molecular-weight fragments increases differentially, so the effective range of separation decreases; to obtain maximum resolution of DNA fragments >2 kb in size, agarose gels should be run at no more than 5–8 V/cm.

subjective.question: Compare agarose and polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis.
subjective.answer: Agarose gels are used to separate larger DNA fragments: DNAs from 50 bp to several megabases in length can be separated on agarose gels of various concentrations and configurations, and as the size of the DNA fragment increases, the percentage of gel has to be decreased; gels cast with low concentrations of agarose (0.1–0.2% w/v) can resolve extremely large DNA molecules. Polyacrylamide gels are most effective for separating small fragments of DNA (5–500 bp) and are run in a vertical configuration in a constant electric field. For extremely large DNA molecules, pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE), developed by Schwartz and Cantor in 1984, is used. Buffers used for native double-stranded DNA include Tris-acetate-EDTA (TAE), Tris-borate (TBE) and Tris-phosphate (TPE); dsDNA migrates about 10% faster through TAE than through TBE or TPE.

subjective.question: What is chromatography? Write its applications.
subjective.answer: Chromatography is an important biophysical technique that enables the separation, identification and purification of the components of a mixture for qualitative and quantitative analysis. A wide range of chromatographic procedures makes use of differences in size, binding affinities, charge and other properties to separate materials. It is a powerful separation tool used in all branches of science. Applications: Pharmaceutical sector — to identify and analyze samples for the presence of trace elements or chemicals, separation of compounds based on molecular weight and element composition, detection of unknown compounds and purity of mixtures, and drug development. Chemical industry — testing water samples and checking air quality. Forensic science — forensic pathology and crime scene testing, e.g. analyzing blood and hair samples. Molecular biology — hyphenated techniques such as EC-LC-MS in metabolomics and proteomics and nucleic acid research; HPLC is used in protein separation like insulin purification, plasma fractionation and enzyme purification.

subjective.question: Describe the components of a TLC (thin layer chromatography) system.
subjective.answer: A TLC system consists of: (1) TLC plates, preferably ready-made with a stationary phase — stable and chemically inert plates on whose whole surface a thin layer of stationary phase of uniform thickness and fine particle size is applied; (2) the TLC chamber, used for the development of the TLC plate — it maintains a uniform environment inside for proper development of spots, prevents the evaporation of solvents and keeps the process dust free; (3) the mobile phase, which comprises a solvent or solvent mixture — it should be particulate-free and of the highest purity for proper development of TLC spots, and the solvents recommended are chemically inert with the sample and the stationary phase; and (4) a filter paper, moistened in the mobile phase and placed inside the chamber, which helps develop a uniform rise of the mobile phase over the length of the stationary phase.
